dialog.body: Public Works, this is Lorraine. How can I help you this afternoon?
Yes, hello. This is Diego Quintero. I am calling about the water again, at the building where I live. Forty-eight Admiral Kalbfus Road, in the North End.
Okay, Mr. Quintero, forty-eight Admiral Kalbfus Road. And you said again, so this has happened before?
Every time it rains hard, every time. And this last weekend, the nor'easter, Saturday into Sunday, it was the worst. Now it is Tuesday and still I have the mess.
Alright. Tell me what you're seeing. Is it the street, or is it on the property?

It is the parking lot, behind the building. The lot goes down toward the back door. All the water runs to the door, and it stands there. The drain in the lot, it is not taking anything. So the water comes to the entrance, and that is the door I use, because the front has the steps and I am eighty-some years old.
I understand. So the lot slopes toward the back entrance and the water pools at the door. Did it get inside the building?

A little, at the bottom of the door, on the mat. I put towels. But mostly it is outside. Wait, one second, my mouse stopped working, I am looking at your website and using this, the trackpad, and I am very bad with it. Excuse me.
That's fine, take your time. You don't need the website for this, I can take the report right here over the phone.
Okay, okay. Good. Then I leave the computer. It was only to find the number, and I found it, and I am on the telephone, so enough.
Perfect. So the water has gone down now, or is it still standing there today?

The water is mostly gone. But the sidewalk, it is a sheet of mud and grit. All of it came out of the lot and the street and it stayed on the sidewalk. When you walk it is like walking on sand over ice. I almost fell yesterday. I use a cane.

Oh, that's not safe at all. Mud and grit on the sidewalk right in front of the back door, and it's the entrance you use. Let me make sure I have this right. The drain in the parking lot behind forty-eight Admiral Kalbfus is clogged or not draining, the lot runs toward the back door, and the sidewalk is covered in silt.
Yes, that is it exactly. You have it right.
Do you know if that drain is on the private lot or if it's a city drain out on the street?
I don't know this. The landlord says it is the city. The city, I think, says it is the landlord. I am only the renter. I only know I am the one who has the water at my door. Excuse me, one moment.
[pause] Ma, é nha telefoni, ka bu preokupa. N ta kaba ligeru. [pause] Sorry. My niece is here, she is asking if I want tea. I said no, I am on the phone.
No problem at all. Go ahead and have your tea if you like, I'm here.

No, no, I want to finish this. So. I want to ask you something. When did they last come by? The city. To clean the drains over here. Because I have not seen a truck, not once this winter, and I have been here a long time.

That's a fair question. I don't have the cleaning schedule in front of me for that spot, and I can't see from here if a crew has been out to Admiral Kalbfus recently. What I can do is put in the request and ask the drain crew to check their records for that area, and to tell us whether that drain belongs to the city.
So you don't know when. Nobody knows when.
I can't tell you the date myself, Mr. Quintero, that's right. But it'll be on the work record, and I'll ask them to put that in the notes so someone can tell you.
Because I called before, you know. Not this winter maybe, but before. And they said they would send somebody. Nobody came. Nobody. And now I am calling again and I am telling you the same story.

I'm sorry about that. I'm not seeing the earlier call from where I am, so I'll write this one up with as much detail as I can, so it doesn't get lost. Can I get a phone number for you in case the crew needs to reach you?
Yes. It is four-oh-one, five-five-five, zero-one-five-four. This is the landline. If I am not answering, my niece sometimes picks up.
Four-oh-one, five-five-five, zero-one-five-four. Got it. And your name is Diego Quintero, Q-U-I-N-T-E-R-O?
Yes, correct. Diego. Like the name in Spanish, but we are from Cape Verde.

Thank you. Now, for the sidewalk, if it's on the public side along the road, the crew may handle the grit when they get to the drain. If it's on the lot, that part may fall to the property owner. I'll note that it's a hazard for someone with a cane, so they treat it with some priority.
Yes, please put that. The cane. Because if I fall, then what? Then you will have a bigger problem than the drain.
Understood. I'm putting in that you're in your eighties, you use a cane, and the back entrance is the one you rely on.
And when will they come? Give me a day. Tomorrow? Thursday?

I wish I could give you a day, but after a storm like this one the crews have a lot of calls stacked up, and I'd be making it up if I named one. What I'd expect is a call or a visit this week, but I can't promise it.
This week. Okay. This is what everybody says. Soon, this week. Me, I have seen the water come to my door five, six times already, and every time the same answer.
I hear you. That's why I want it written clearly. Is there anything else about the lot? Is the drain covered with leaves, or is it a grate you can see?
It is a grate, a metal one, in the middle of the lot, lower than the rest. It is full of leaves and the sand, packed. I looked at it with my cane. Nothing goes down.
Okay, a metal grate in the low part of the lot, packed with leaves and sand. That helps the crew a lot.
And the landlord, he doesn't answer when I call him. So I call you.
That's all right, that's what we're here for. If it turns out it's private, I'll ask the crew to let you know so you can take it back to the owner with that information. Would that help?
Yes, that helps. At least then I have something to say to him. Not just that I am an old man complaining.

You're not complaining for nothing, this is a real hazard. Let me read it all back. Forty-eight Admiral Kalbfus Road, North End. Parking lot behind the building slopes toward the back door. The lot drain is clogged and the water pools at the entrance after storms, most recently last weekend's nor'easter. Sidewalk is covered in mud and grit, and you're asking when the drains in that area were last cleaned. Callback at four-oh-one, five-five-five, zero-one-five-four.
Yes. Yes, that is all. Very good. You repeat everything good.
I like to be sure. If it gets worse, say the water starts coming into the hallway, or the sidewalk freezes over with that grit in it, call back right away and mention this report.
Okay. I will call. Do not worry, I will call. [pause] My niece says I should say thank you. So, thank you.
You're welcome, Mr. Quintero. Tell her thank you too, and please be careful on that walk.
I will be careful. Goodbye.
Goodbye now.
